abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is the most prevalent subtype of lung cancer. Previous studies have highlighted the critical roles of complement and coagulation cascades in tumor development, maintenance, and therapeutic response. However, the overall impact of complement and coagulation cascade-related (CCCR) genes on LUAD progression and their role in the tumor microenvironment (TME) remain insufficiently explored. Therefore, we screened CCCR genes with important roles in LUAD using RNA sequencing data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Subsequently, a prognostic model, based on 8 hub genes (IGFBP1, TUBB, PLEK2, CNTNAP2, CPS1, EREG, CENPE, HBEGF) identified using the Lasso-Cox algorithm, was developed to stratify LUAD patients into high- and low-risk groups. This model demonstrated strong predictive capability and calibration, with an AUC of 0.816 in the external validation cohort. Multiomics clustering revealed that 2 cancer subtypes (CSs) are associated with prognosis, with CS2 demonstrating the most favorable prognostic outcome and validating the validity of the prognostic model. Additionally, we analyzed the immune infiltration, tumor mutation burden (TMB) and immunophenoscore (IPS) of the riskscore in the models. Through this analysis, we have identified for the first time CCCR genes are highly associated with clinical characteristics, immune cell infiltration patterns, and immune therapeutic responses of LUAD. This prognostic model constructed based on CCCR genes represents a valid tool for the prognosis of LUAD patients. Our findings provide valuable insights into the prognostic and immunological relevance of CCCR genes in LUAD, offering a robust foundation for personalized treatment strategies and future research.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Tumor is the leading cause of death worldwide, with lung cancer being the most common and lethal form of cancer in humans [1]. Lung cancer is categorized into small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) being the most prevalent subtype of NSCLC [2]. As the largest subtype of NSCLC, LUAD requires more in-depth research to improve our understanding and treatment strategies. LUAD is currently treated with various therapeutic approaches, including surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and targeted therapy, with the efficacy of treatment further enhanced by the advent of immunotherapy [3, 4]. Over the past decade, the development of immunotherapies for patients with high expression of programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) has shown considerable success, with the clinical use of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) significantly improving survival outcomes for these patients [5]. However, despite these therapeutic advancements, it is important to recognize that outcomes for many LUAD patients remain unsatisfactory, largely due to the complexity of the tumor microenvironment (TME), which presents a significant barrier to effective treatment [6]. The TME represents the immediate ecological niche surrounding the tumor, comprising a variety of cells [7, 8]. In the TME, both immune and stromal cells interact with tumor cells to modulate their behaviour. Certain immunosuppressive mechanisms within the TME can hinder therapeutic immune responses [9]. Complement and coagulation cascade (CCC) reactions are increasingly recognized as critical regulators of the TME, particularly through their influence on immune cell infiltration and cancer progression. Previous studies [10, 11] have indicated that dysregulation of complement and coagulation factors can reshape the immune landscape of tumors, contributing to immune suppression and poor clinical outcomes. For instance, tissue factor (F3) reduces the recognition and clearance of tumor cells by NK cells [12], thereby promoting immune escape. Initially considered two separate biological processes, the complement and coagulation systems were now understood to interact extensively [13]. Research has increasingly highlighted their interdependence, with activation of either system potentially triggering or exacerbating the response of the other, forming a complex positive feedback interaction. This cycle involves the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) [14], promoting tumorigenesis, progression and metastasis. Based on these findings, we believe that complement and coagulation cascade-related (CCCR) genes may be critically involved in shaping immune infiltration and influencing patient prognosis in LUAD. However, the prognostic significance and immunological roles of CCCR genes in LUAD remain largely unexplored. In recent years, the application of machine learning and multi-omics technologies in both medicine and pharmacology has greatly accelerated the discovery of disease mechanisms and biomarkers, enabling more precise and large-scale exploration of complex biological systems[15–17]. Therefore, further investigation of CCCR genes using bioinformatics approaches is imperative to evaluate the progression and prognosis of LUAD.

In this study, based on TCGA-LUAD and GEO databases, we performed multiomics analysis of CCCR genes by machine learning and screened the risk genes and their coefficients, which are closely related to the progression of LUAD, and established and validated the risk model. Furthermore, we explored the association between the riskscore and factors such as immune infiltration, immune checkpoint genes, and response to immunotherapy in LUAD patients. This provides a rationale for early intervention in LUAD patients, particularly regarding coagulation and cascade responses. Figure 1 shows the general framework of this study.

sec.title: Identification of DEGs
sec.p: Through differential analysis of tumor and normal tissues from the TCGA-LUAD dataset, we identified 1,962 differential genes (DEGs) (Fig. 2A,B), including 1361 up-regulated genes and 601 down-regulated genes. Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment illustrated the functional characteristics of DEGs across three perspectives: biological process (BP), cellular component (CC), and molecular function (MF) enrichment (Fig. 2D). In BP, DEGs were primarily involved in external encapsulating structure organization and extracellular matrix organization; In CC, DEGs were mainly enriched in the nucleosome and collagen-containing extracellular matrix; in MF, DEGs were mainly enriched in structural constituent chromatin and glycosaminoglycan binding. Additionally, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis (Fig. 2C) indicated that, besides the CCC pathway, DEGs were significantly enriched in various tumorigenesis-related pathways, such as neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, cell cycle, and cAMP signaling pathway.

B Venn diagram illustrated the overlapping genes between the DEGs and CCCR genes, identifying 442 intersecting genes. C GO analysis of the 442 intersecting CCCR genes. D KEGG analysis of the 442 intersecting CCCR genes. E PPI network map of the 442 intersecting CCCR genes. F The top 24 genes were ranked by degree, which represents the number of direct interactions each gene has within the PPI network

sec.title: PPI network construction
sec.p: To explore the interactions among the 442 differentially expressed CCCR genes, the STRING database was first analysed. The interactions were visualized as a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network (Fig. 2E) using Cytoscape software.

For the PPI network, we performed a degree-based visualization (Fig. 2F) and identified several key genes, including CDK1, CCN2A2, CCNB1, BUB1B, BUB1, TOP2A, ALB, F2, BIRCF2, BIRC5, PLK1, CENPE, AURKB and other genes. Genes with higher degree values have more interactions and are considered central hubs, which are potentially critical for maintaining network integrity and biological functions. Although some of the top genes (such as CDK1 and CCNB1) are not traditional members of the CCC pathway, they still occupy central positions in the PPI network. This suggests a potential link between cell cycle mechanisms [18, 19] and the CCC pathway in LUAD. These genes can play pivotal roles in the pathophysiologic mechanisms underlying the CCC in LUAD.

sec.title: Multiomics integration analysis
sec.p: To explore the multiomics characteristics of CCCR-genes in LUAD patients, the MOVICS [17] package for multiomics integrated clustering analysis was utilised. This approach enabled the identification of two cancer subtypes (CSs) (Fig. 3A-C) by 10 multiomics integrated clustering algorithms, analyzing mRNA, microRNA, methylation and mutation profiles of CCCR genes. The results demonstrated that our classification system strongly correlated with overall survival (OS) in both the TCGA-LUAD cohort and GSE50081 (; Fig. 2D,F). Notably, cancer subtype 1 (CS1) exhibited the most favourable survival outcomes among all subtypes evaluated. To further validate the consistency of the clustering methods, we performed consistency assessment among different methods. The Kappa coefficient was utilised to assess clustering consistency between CSs and NTP, yielding a result of 0.752 (Supplementary Fig.1A). Similarly, the consistency between CSs and PAM was 0.779 (Supplementary Fig.1B), while the consistency between NTP and PAM reached 0.890 (Supplementary Fig.1C). All of these values exhibited a remark ably high degree of consistency (). These findings further substantiate the reliability of the clustering analysis and the sample grouping methodologies employed.

caption.p: The multiomics integrative consensus subtypes of CCCR genes. A Comprehensive heatmap of consensus ensemble subtypes, including mRNA, miRNA, DNA CpG methylation sites, and mutant genes. B Clustering of LUAD patients using 10 cutting-edge multiomics clustering methods. C Consensus clustering matrix for two novel prognostic subtypes based on the 10 algorithms. D Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of two subtypes in the TCGA-LUAD cohort. E Boxplot of riskscore for the two subtypes in the TCGA-LUAD cohort. F Survival outcomes among the two subtypes in the GSE50081 cohort. G Boxplot of riskscore for the two subtypes in the GSE50081 cohort

sec.title: The construction of a signature model
sec.p: Following the implementation of LASSO regression analysis on a total of 422 DEGs associated with CCC, lasso.min identified eight genes. The final formula obtained for calculating the The riskscore was calculated using the following formula:

The median of the riskscore was used as the cutoff point to stratify patients into high-risk and low-risk groups. Kaplan-Meier analysis revealed that the low-risk group exhibited a significantly higher survival probability than the high-risk group within the training set (Fig. 4E; ). Moreover, patients’ survival time showed a decreasing trend with increasing riskscore(Fig. 4C), and the riskscore of dead cases was significantly higher than that of alive cases. (; Fig. 4D). Similarly, the findings were consistent in the TESTING set GSE72094 and GSE50081 (Fig. 4G,I,K). Furthermore, time-ROC curves were plotted for LUAD patients at 1, 3, and 5 years. The area under the curve (AUC) for the time-ROC curves in the TRAINING SET were 0.795, 0.761, and 0.716 respectively (Fig. 4F), while the TESTING SET showed comparable results: 1-year, 3-year, and 5-year AUCs were 0.755, 0.7, and 0.648 (Fig. 4H), respectively. These results indicated that the risk model demonstrated robust predictive effect on the survival of LUAD patients at 1, 3, and 5 years. Subsequent external validation based on GSE50081 and GSE72094 further confirmed the reliability of the model. ROC analysis for predicting 1-, 3-, and 5-year OS rates yielded AUCs of 0.816, 0.717, and 0.7 for GSE50081 (Fig. 4J) and 0.691, 0.647, and 0.707 for GSE72094 (Fig. 4L). Concurrently, survival analysis in these cohorts (Fig. 4E,G,I,K) demonstrated that patients in the high-risk group exhibited a significantly poorer prognosis compared to those in the low-risk group (). Notably, this risk model could be applied successfully to the multi-omics clustering model, with the riskscore for CS2 subtypes being significantly higher than that for CS1 subtypes in both TCGA-LAUD and GSE50081 (; Fig. 2E,G).

sec.title: Association between clinicopathological factors and riskscore in patients with LUAD
sec.p: To further explore the correlation between the riskscore and patient prognosis, an evaluation was made of the correlation between riskscore and clinical stage of LUAD patients. The analysis revealed that the riskscore was significantly correlated with stage T, stage N, and Stage (; Fig. 5C-F). However, the riskscore was not a strong predictor of distant metastases (stage M) and between stage N3, which can be attributed to the small sample size for these stages, as only 1 out of 340 samples for N3 (Table 1), and only 22 patients had stage M1. Therefore, the predictive performance of the risk model is relatively limited in patients in the late-stages of LUAD. Furthermore, to better conduct the molecular mechanisms through which the riskscore affects prognosis, we explored relevant pathways that promote tumorigenesis and progression. As illustrated in (Fig. 5I) and supplementary table 1, numerous pathways were significantly enriched in the high-risk group, including the HALLMARK_E2F_TARGETS, HALLMARK_G2M_CHECKPOINT and several others. These findings highlight the critical molecular pathways involved in the pathophysiology of LUAD. This finding indicates that substantial variations in stage T, stage N, and STAGE were observed alongside elevated riskscore, suggesting that the riskscore not only serves as a prognostic indicator for LUAD patients but also correlates with their clinicopathologic characteristics. Consequently, it holds potential as a valuable instrument for evaluating patient staging and prognosis.

sec.title: Establishment and validation of a nomogram model
sec.p: To construct a prognostic model, a search for independent prognostic factors was initially conducted. Uni-variate and multi-variate Cox regression (Fig. 5A,B) were then performed for age, gender, stage and riskscore, respectively. In the TCGA-LUAD cohort, Stage and riskscore were identified as significant independent prognostic factors affecting LUAD prognosis. Among these factors, the hazard ratio of riskscore was significantly higher than that of any other parameter, further confirming the reliability of the risk model. Subsequently, a nomogram was developed to predict 1-, 3-, and 5-year OS for LUAD patients. This nomogram (Fig. 5G) utilised independent prognostic factors identified by multi-variate COX analysis, alongside clinically recognised factors such as age. The P-value for the model was , and the C-index was determined to be 0.7238 (95% CI = 0.7047–0.7429). These findings indicate that the model possesses excellent predictive ability and reliability.

sec.title: Immune infiltration analysis
sec.p: To further validate the correlation between riskscore and TME, the ESTIMATE algorithm was utilised to assess immune infiltration of TME. The results demonstrated that the Immunescore and ESTIMATEscore of the low-risk group were significantly higher than those of the high-risk group (Fig. 7A,C), indicating that the low-risk group exhibited higher immunoreactivity and a stronger immune response. Meanwhile, the tumorpurity of the high-risk group was significantly higher than that of the low-risk group (Fig. 7D), suggesting that the high-risk group contained a richer tumor cell component, which might be associated with immune escape or immunosuppressive features of the tumor microenvironment. The CIBERSORT algorithm was used to analyze the proportion of tumor-infiltrating immune subpopulations. The results of immune infiltration showed that riskscore was positively correlated with T cells CD4 memory activated, macrophages M0, NK cells resting, Macrophages.M1, mast cells activated, neutrophils, dendritic cells activated cells positively correlated (; Fig. 6A-H). Conversely, a negative correlation was observed between riskscore and B. cells memory, tregs, mast cells resting, monocytes and dendritic cells resting (Fig. 6I-O). Moreover, significant differences in immune cell proportions, including B cells memory, T cells CD4 memory activated, T cells CD4 memory resting and other immune cells, were observed between the high- and low-risk groups(; Fig. 6P).

caption.p: Immune function and immunotherapy response analysis of the CCCR gene signature in the TCGA-LUAD cohort. A–D Stromal score, immune score, and ESTIMATE score levels in different risk groups, evaluated using the ESTIMATE algorithm. E Expression profiles of ICGs between high-risk and low-risk groups. F Immunophenoscore (IPS) comparisons across different risk groups

The CIBERSORT algorithm was applied to evaluate the distribution of 22 immune cell types. A–O Scatter plot showed the correlation of 15 kinds of immune cells proportion with the riskscore (p <0.05). Pearson coefficient was used for the correlation test. P Scatter plot showed the ratio differentiation of 22 kinds of immune cells between LUAD tumor samples with low or high-risk group, and Wilcoxon rank sum was used for the significance test

sec.title: Evaluation of immunotherapeutic effects
sec.p: Further comparison of immune checkpoint genes (ICGs) expression between the high-risk and low-risk groups revealed significant variations in the expression of numerous ICGs (; Fig. 7E). Most of these ICGs showed higher expression in the low-risk group, which may contribute to the better prognosis observed in this group. Subsequently, we further analyzed the IPS obtained from the TCIA database. A higher IPS indicated that the patients had a better response to ICI treatment. The results showed that for low-risk group the IPS in CTLA4-/PD1-, CTLA4+/PD1-, CTLA4-/PD1+ were significantly higher than that of high-risk group (Fig. 7F), which suggested that patients with lower riskscore can gain more benefit from single-agent immunotherapy.

sec.title: TMB analysis
sec.p: TMB was evaluated in TCGA-LUAD using the maftools package, which was used to analyse the data and generate the mutation profile (Fig. 8A). The results demonstrated that missense mutation was the most prevalent in LUAD, with SNP being the most common variant type. Major mutated genes included TTN, MUC16, CSMD3 and so on. In addition, an exploration was conducted into the mutation status of the genes selected by LASSO regression, and their respective mutation profiles were depicted. Figure 8C shows that CNTNAP2 and CENPE have the highest mutation frequencies in the LASSO regression model. Concurrently, the TMB of the high-risk group was significantly higher than that of the low-risk group (; Fig. 8B), suggesting that higher riskscore may be associated with more aggressive lung adenocarcinoma subtypes, leading to increased tumor malignancy and greater treatment challenges.

caption.p: Mutation analysis in LUAD. A Overview plot of gene mutations. B Total mutation burden (TMB) in different risk groups. C Mutation landscape of genes selected by the LASSO regression model

sec.title: Data acquisition
sec.p: We obtained mRNA expression profiles of 513 cases of lung adenocarcinoma and 58 cases of normal tissue from the TCGA database using the R package “TCGAbiolinks”. After excluding samples with missing data on survival status, survival time, gender, age, T stage, N stage, M stage, and Stage, a total of 340 LUAD cases with complete clinical and pathological information were obtained. In addition, methylation data, gene mutation data, and miRNA data from the TCGA database (https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/) and xena (https://xena.ucsc.edu/) for multi-omics analysis. Relevant data from the GEO database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/) were also obtained, including 127 cases from the GSE50081 dataset and 398 cases from the GSE72094 dataset. Samples with missing or low-quality omics data were excluded from further analysis to ensure data completeness and reliability. Data normalization was achieved by R package “limma” to ensure the removal of batch effects. The data were then analyzed. A total of 3,765 CCCR genes were retrieved from Genecards (https://www.genecards.org/), as listed in the supplementary table 2.

sec.title: Identification of DEGs
sec.p: We used the R package “DESeq2” to analyze the differential expression between normal and tumor samples in TCGA-LUAD. The significance criteria were set at and . The results were visualized using the R packages “pheatmap”, “ggpubr” and “ggthemes”.

sec.title: Functional enrichment analyses and PPI
sec.p: We performed GO and KEGG enrichment analysis on the DEGs between tumor and normal tissues in TCGA-LUAD using the R package “ClusterProfiler”. The significance thresholds were set at , . PPI were analysed using the STRING database (http://www.string-db.org/) and visualized by Cytoscape (version 3.9.0) software.

sec.title: Multiomics analysis
sec.p: To explore the multiomics data features of CCCR genes in LUAD patients, R package “MOVICS” was utilised for the purpose of conducting multiomics integrated cluster analysis based on 442 differentially expressed CCCR genes. The mRNA, miRNA, methylation and mutation data of TCGA-LUAD patients were subjected to a thorough cleaning process to ensure the quality of the data prior to performing a multiomics analysis. Specifically, we focused on 442 differentially expressed CCCR genes, and applied MOVICS’s built-in functions for feature selection and clustering. For mRNA, miRNA, and methylation data, features were selected based on Cox proportional hazards regression (), and for miRNA data, MAD-based filtering was also applied to ensure variability. Mutation data were filtered based on mutation frequency (top 10%). The optimal number of clusters was estimated by evaluating cluster numbers ranging from 2 to 8 based on internal clustering validity metrics. Multi-omics clustering was then performed using ten state-of-the-art algorithms implemented in MOVICS: SNF, CIMLR, PINSPlus, NEMO, COCA, MoCluster, LRAcluster, ConsensusClustering, IntNMF, and iClusterBayes. The robustness of clustering was assessed using consensus clustering and Kappa coefficient analysis. This process was subsequently validated using the GSE50081. Moreover, clustering stability was further validated through consistency assessment across methods using Kappa coefficient analysis.

sec.title: The construction of the signature model
sec.p: The TCGA-LUAD samples were randomly split into a training set (n=170) and a testing set (n=170) at a ratio of 1:1. The split was performed in a completely random manner without stratification. Using the training set, we first screened the differentially expressed CCCR genes with prognostic value by univariate Cox regression. These candidate genes were further subjected to LASSO Cox regression modeling using the “glmnet” R package. A 10-fold cross-validation procedure was applied to identify the optimal regularization parameter lambda. We selected lambda.min, which corresponds to the value of lambda that yielded the minimum mean cross-validated error, to construct the prognostic model. Risk genes and their coefficients were extracted accordingly. Based on the median riskscore, we categorized LUAD patients into high-risk and low-risk groups. Kaplan-Meier Survival analysis was performed using the R packages “survival” and “survminer” to evaluate the prognosis of these two groups. Time-ROC curves for 1, 3, and 5 years survival were plotted using the “timeROC” package. We performed internal validation using the test set and further external validation using data from GSE50081 and GSE72094 to finalize the reliability of the model.

sec.title: The construction of nomogram
sec.p: The present study investigated the relationship between the riskscore and clinical variables. The riskscore was combined with several clinical characteristics, and both univariate and multivariate-Cox regression analyses were performed to assess the independent prognostic value for LUAD patients. The results were visualized using the “forestplot” package. Furthermore, a nomogram was developed utilising the results derived from multifactorial regression analyses, employing the package “rms”. The objective of this development was to estimate the probability of 1-, 3-, and 5-year OS in patients diagnosed with LUAD. The predictive efficacy of the nomogram was evaluated using the C-index and calibration curves.

sec.title: Gene set enrichment analysis
sec.p: To explore potential risk mechanisms between high-risk and low-risk groups, the GSEA algorithm was used for further study. and were considered statistically significant and visualized using the “enrichplot” package.

sec.title: Evaluation of immune infiltration characteristics
sec.p: To explore the relationship between riskscores and the immune microenvironment, the differences in the immune microenvironment between the high-risk and low-risk groups were quantified and visualized, with particular emphasis on the distribution of tumor-infiltrating immune cells. We performed CIBERSORT analysis with 100 permutations (perm = 100) on all samples and visualized the relative proportions of all 22 immune cell types. Additionally, the “ESTIMATE” package was employed to estimate the proportions of immune stromal components in the TME of each sample, generating three distinct scores:ImmuneScore, StromalScore, and ESTIMATEScore. These scores are positively correlated with the ratio of immune, stromal, and the sum of the two, respectively. Higher scores indicate a greater proportion of immune or stromal components, which corresponds to less tumorpurity.

sec.title: Correlations between riskscore and ICGs and IPS
sec.p: To assess the relationship between riskscores and immunotherapy, we first evaluated the association between riskscores and ICGs. According to the study by Fei-Fei Hu [20], 79 ICGs (supplementary table 3) were selected for further study. These genes are primarily involved in ligand, receptor or immune checkpoint pathways. Immunotherapy-related data of LUAD patients in TCGA-LUAD was obtained from The Cancer Immunome Database (TCIA; https://tcia.at/home), and the association between riskscores and IPS was further evaluated.

sec.title: Mutation analysis
sec.p: The TMB data for the TCGA-LUAD samples was obtained from the TCGA database and subsequently processed. The processed data were then visualized using the “maftools” package. TMB was expressed as mutations per megabase (mut/Mb), using a capture size of 50 Mb to represent the exome.

sec.title: Statistics
sec.p: All statistical analyses were conducted utilising RStudio(version 4.0.5), employing a range of statistical methodologies, encompassing the Wilcoxon test and the Log-rank test. The symbol * indicates , ** indicates , and *** indicates .

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: LUAD is characterized by high morbidity and mortality, exhibiting significant metastatic potential, tumor heterogeneity, and a complex response to immunotherapy. The CCC play a crucial role in tumorigenesis and progression [13, 14]. However, the correlation between the CCCR gene and LUAD prognosis and TME, has not been comprehensively explored. Therefore, investigating the role of CCCR gene in LUAD is both scientifically valuable and urgently needed. In this study, we explored multiomics analysis to identify the molecular subtypes of CCCR genes and found that this classification system was closely associated with patients’ OS. We validated the reliability of the model in the TCGA-LUAD and GSE50081 cohorts. Using LASSO regression, we constructed a risk model capable of accurately assessing the prognosis of LUAD patients. The model, which relies on a limited number of gene expression levels to calculate a patient’s riskscore, offers a valuable tool for physicians to identify high-risk patients and ensure that they benefit from more comprehensive screening and treatment. We found that the riskscore was closely associated with patient prognosis and several key clinical characteristics. Statistical analyses showed that patients in the high-risk group had significantly worse survival outcomes than those in the low-risk group, and that the risk scores of deceased patients were significantly higher than those of the high-risk group. These associations were consistently validated across the training cohort, the internal validation set, and two external validation datasets. Moreover, the riskscore was strongly correlated with T stage, N stage, and overall clinical stage (TNM classification), further highlighting the clinical relevance of the CCCR-based risk model. In summary, this study not only constructed an effective prognostic model but also revealed the important biological significance of the CCCR gene in LUAD, providing new theoretical support for individualized treatment and early intervention.

In this study, we selected eight characteristic genes - IGFBP1, TUBB, PLEK2, CNTNAP2, CPS1, EREG, CENPE, and HBEGF - and constructed a risk model capable of accurately assessing the prognosis of LUAD patients. Previous studies have shown that IGFBP1 plays an important role in various cancers, particularly in lung adenocarcinoma, where its high expression is associated with tumor metastasis and poorer prognosis [21, 22], which is consistent with our findings. IGFBP1 not only promotes cell proliferation and migration but also regulates tumor cell growth through the PPAR pathway [22]. Furthermore, the role of PLEK2 in NSCLC has garnered significant attention. Studies have shown that PLEK2 promotes NSCLC proliferation and metastasis through a BRD4-dependent mechanism [23]. Overexpression of PLEK2 also promotes epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and cell migration in NSCLC [24]. High expression of TUBB in various tumors is typically associated with poor prognosis, especially in LUAD, where its overexpression correlates with poorer survival and chemotherapy resistance [25, 26]. Genes related to the complement and coagulation cascades jointly regulate tumor cell activity. For example, EREG, one of the eight genes studied in this research, is overexpressed in multiple cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) [27]. In NSCLC, EREG can activate EGFR, thereby activating the EGFR-AkT pathway during the occurrence and development of lung cancer [27].

CENPE maintains high expression in a wide range of tumors [28] and plays a crucial role in the TME by significantly influencing a variety of immune cell types, including T-helper cells, mast cells, Th2 cells, Tcm, and others [29]. In addition, EREG is pivotal in the EMT process of tumor cells, especially in NSCLC, where elevated EREG expression is associated with poorer prognosis [30]. High expression of CPS1 in lung adenocarcinoma patients correlates with shorter OS, with its hypomethylation potentially contributing to its overexpression [31]. In KRAS/LKB1-mutant lung cancer cells, CPS1 promotes DNA synthesis by maintaining pyrimidine pool homeostasis, thereby supporting cell proliferation and survival, especially in certain lung adenocarcinoma subtypes [32].

CCCR genes are clearly linked to immune cell infiltration in the TME of LUAD patients. Notably, we noticed that T cells CD4 memory were prevalent in the high-risk group, while resting memory T cells CD4 memory were more abundant in the low-risk group. Previous studies have shown that the degree of infiltration of memory CD4+ T cell is strongly correlated with cancer progression. Voigt et al [33] showed that in TME, T cells CD4 memory can be induced by interleukin- 22 to produce interleukin- 1, effectively promoting tumor growth. Similarly, in LUAD patients, CD4+ T cells cell-associated genes were significantly enriched in signalling pathways such as cell cycle, p53 signalling pathway and glutathione metabolism [34]. This may partially explain the poorer prognosis observed in the high-risk group.

Previous studies [35] have demonstrated that in certain types of cancer, Eosinophils and mast cells are more abundant during the precancerous and early stages of the tumor, whereas their numbers decrease in the advanced stages.This observation aligns with our findings. In the early stages of the tumor, the number and activation of eosinophils and mast cells are elevated, contributing to the inhibition of tumor progression. As the tumor advances, however, the number of these cells gradually decreases, which may suggest their active involvement in mediating anti-tumor effects [35].

NK cells are well-known for their tumor-suppressive roles in immune surveillance, capable of directly or indirectly eliminating tumor cells through a variety of pathways. However, in the present study, we observed a higher number of NK cells in the high-risk group. This may be explained by the consistent suppression of NK cells [36, 37]. For example, NK cells within the TME of breast cancer were found to be immature, exhibiting reduced expression of DX5, CD27CD11b phenotype, increased expression of NKG2A, and low levels of NKp46, perforin and granzyme B [38]. At the same time, Complement iC3b can negatively regulate NK cells by reducing their production of IFN - [39, 40]. In addition, the impact of the complement system on neutrophils cannot be ignored. Sergio Ortiz Espinosa’s research [41] suggests that C5a, a component of the complement system, promotes the production of neutrophil extracellular traps, thereby facilitating tumor spread.

However, several limitations must be acknowledged in our study. Firstly, the results were based on public databases and bioinformatics analyses. Although a variety of scientific methods were employed to analyze the data, these results have not been validated through cell and animal experiments. Secondly, the limited number of advanced LUAD patients (stage IV) included in the model restricts its ability to reliably predict the prognosis of advanced patients. Therefore, future studies should incorporate more clinical data as well as basic research to further assess the applied value of these findings.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In this study, we systematically demonstrated through bioinformatics analysis that the CCCR gene holds significant prognostic value in LUAD and explored its potential impact on immune cell infiltration. Furthermore, a robust prognostic model based on the CCCR gene was constructed. The results of this study provide a new theoretical foundation and research direction for the development of individualised treatment strategies and early intervention in LUAD patients.
